\section{Schrodinger model}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger:schrodinger-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger::doc}}\subsubsection*{Contents}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-analytical-sln}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Mathematical details of the analytical solution}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-gallery}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Gallery of orbitals}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Auxiliary notes}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Schrodinger equation.} Schrodinger equation in space basis for the electron in a \(\text{H}\) atom reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \partial_t \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) = \left[ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \right] \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \ \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the Hamiltonian is the sum of the kinetic energy and a Coulomb potential contribution, \(\hat{V}\), so that \(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{V} | \Psi \rangle = - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon |\mathbf{r}|} \Psi(\mathbf{r},t)\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spectral decomposition of the Hamiltonian operator.} The stationary states, and the corresponding energy levels \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. the eigenfunctions, and the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian operator \(\hat{H}\) \sphinxhyphen{} are the result of the eigenvalue problem, \(\hat{H} | \Psi \rangle = E | \Psi \rangle\), or using space basis,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left[ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \right] \Psi(\mathbf{r}) = E \Psi(\mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Quantum numbers.} The stationary states depend on \sphinxstylestrong{three} \sphinxhyphen{} in this model, no spin exists \sphinxhyphen{} \sphinxstylestrong{quantum numbers}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{principal} quantum number \(n \in \{ 1, 2, \dots \}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{azimuthal} quantum number \(\ell \in \{ 0, 1,\dots, n-1 \} \)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{magnetic} quantum number \(m_{\ell} \in \{ -\ell, -\ell+1, \dots, \ell \}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Energy levels only depend on the principal quantum number, \(E(n)\). Thus, Schrodinger model of the atom has \sphinxstylestrong{degenerate} stationary states, i.e. stationary states with the same energy value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Commutation of \(\hat{H}\), \(\hat{L}^2\), \(\hat{L}_z\).} As angular momentum operators \(\hat{L}^2\), \(\hat{L}_z\) commute with the Hamiltonian operator \(\hat{H}\) of the \(\text{H}\) atom, these three operators share common eigenvectors. These relations are proved in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{note section}}}}.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Schrodinger model \sphinxhyphen{} Mathematical details of the analytical solution}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:schrodinger-model-mathematical-details-of-the-analytical-solution}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-analytical-sln}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Schrodinger equation} for the hydrogen atom in space basis reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) = \left[ - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \nabla^2 - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{r} \right] \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{eigenproblem of the Hermitian operator} (projected onto space basis, as well) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_n \Psi_n(\mathbf{r}) = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \nabla^2 \Psi_n(\mathbf{r}) - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon r} \Psi_n(\mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Given the symmetries of the system, the solution of the eigenproblem is evaluated using spherical coordinates \(\{ r, \theta, \varphi \}\), and the method of separation of variables. Using \sphinxstylestrong{spherical coordinates},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}- \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \left\{ \frac{1}{r^2} \partial_r \left( r^2 \partial_r \right) + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin\theta} \partial_\theta \left( \sin\theta \partial_\theta \right) + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin^2\theta} \partial_{\varphi\varphi} \right\} \Psi_n - \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r} \Psi_n = E_n \Psi_n\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Separation of variables, \protect\(\ \Psi_{nlm}(r, \theta, \varphi) = R_n(r) Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi) \ \protect\) }

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the \sphinxstylestrong{method of separation of variables}, we look for solutions in product form:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Psi_{nlm}(r, \theta, \varphi) = R_n(r) Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and substituting into the Schrödinger equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( E_n + \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r} \right) R_n Y_{lm} = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \left[ \frac{1}{r^2} \left( r^2 R_n' \right)' Y_{lm} + R_n \left( \frac{1}{r^2 \sin\theta} \partial_\theta \left( \sin\theta \partial_\theta Y_{lm} \right) + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin^2\theta} \partial_{\varphi\varphi} Y_{lm} \right) \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dividing by \(R_n Y_{lm}\), and multiplying by \(r^2 \frac{2m}{\hbar^2}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \underbrace{\frac{1}{R_n} (r^2 R_n')' + \frac{2m r^2}{\hbar^2} \left( E_n + \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r} \right)}_{f(r)} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{Y_{lm}} \left\{ \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \partial_\theta (\sin\theta \partial_\theta Y_{lm}) + \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta} \partial_{\varphi\varphi} Y_{lm} \right\}}_{g(\theta, \varphi)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(f(r) + g(\theta, \varphi) = 0\), both terms must equal equal\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}opposite constant \(C\) for all valid domains \(r \in (0, +\infty)\), \(\theta \in (0, \pi)\), \(\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}C = f(r) = - g(\theta, \varphi) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Radial equation, and energy levels}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The radial component determines the energy level,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:eq:atom:schrodinger:energy}
\begin{split}E_n = - \frac{m q^4}{32 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0^2 \hbar^2} \frac{1}{n^2} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(n \in \{ 1, 2, \dots \}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The radial distribution of the energy state functions is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) = e^{-\rho/2} \rho^{\ell} L^{2 \ell+1}_{n-\ell-1}(\rho) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\rho = r \frac{\sqrt{-8 m E_n}}{\hbar}\) the non dimensional radius, \(\ell \in \{ 0, 1, \dots, n-1 \}\), and \(L_{p}^{k}(x)\) the solution of the associated Laguerre differential equation \(x y'' + ( k + 1 - x ) y' + p y = 0\).
\subsubsection*{Change of variables, and asymptotic behavior}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Defining \(C = \ell(\ell+1)\), and dividing the equation \(f(r) = C\) by \(r^2\), for the states with \(E_n <0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d}{dr} \left( r^2 R' \right) + \left[ \frac{2m}{\hbar^2} \left( E + \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r} \right) - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{r^2} \right] R = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Defining the \sphinxstylestrong{dimensionless radial variable} \(\rho = \kappa r\), so \(\frac{d}{dr} = \kappa \frac{d}{d\rho}\), and factoring out \(\kappa^2\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \kappa^2 \left\{ \frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{d}{d\rho} \left( \rho^2 \frac{dR}{d\rho} \right) + \left( \frac{2m E}{\hbar^2 \kappa^2} + \frac{2m q^2}{\hbar^2 \kappa \cdot 4\pi \varepsilon_0 \rho} - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{\rho^2} \right) \right\} R\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By choosing \(\kappa^2 = -\frac{8 m E}{\hbar^2}\) (where \(\kappa = \frac{\sqrt{-8 m E}}{\hbar}\) for \(E < 0\)), the first term inside the parentheses becomes \(-1\). Defining the constant parameter \(\rho_0\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho_0 = \frac{2m q^2}{\hbar^2 \kappa \cdot 4\pi \varepsilon_0} = \frac{2m q^2}{\hbar^2 \sqrt{-8 m E} \cdot 4\pi \varepsilon_0} = \frac{q^2}{8\pi \varepsilon_0 \hbar} \sqrt{\frac{2m}{-E}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the dimensionless radial equation simplifies to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{d}{d\rho} \left( \rho^2 \frac{dR}{d\rho} \right) + R \left[ - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{\rho^2} - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{\rho_0}{\rho} \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Boundary conditions required for regular wavefunctions:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho = 0) < \infty, \quad R(\rho \to +\infty) = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Asymptotic behavior for \protect\(\ r \rightarrow 0\protect\), and \protect\(\ r \rightarrow +\infty\protect\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Large Distance Limit (\(\rho \to +\infty\)).} For large \(\rho\), terms proportional to \(\frac{1}{\rho}\) and \(\frac{1}{\rho^2}\) become negligible:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{d}{d\rho} \left( \rho^2 R' \right) = R'' + \frac{2}{\rho} R' \sim R''\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The equation reduces to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R'' - \frac{1}{4} R \sim 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
General solution:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) = A e^{-\rho/2} + B e^{\rho/2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To satisfy the non\sphinxhyphen{}divergent boundary condition at infinity, set \(B = 0\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) \sim e^{-\rho/2} \quad \text{as } \rho \to +\infty\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Small Distance Limit (\(\rho \to 0\)).} For \(\rho \to 0\), the centrifugal term \(\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{\rho^2}\) dominates over the constant and \(\frac{1}{\rho}\) terms:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R'' + \frac{2}{\rho} R' - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{\rho^2} R \sim 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Proposing a power\sphinxhyphen{}law ansatz \(R(\rho) \sim \rho^s\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s(s - 1) \rho^{s-2} + 2s \rho^{s-2} - \ell(\ell + 1) \rho^{s-2} = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s^2 + s - \ell(\ell + 1) = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Solving the quadratic characteristic equation for \(s\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_{1,2} = \frac{-1 \mp \sqrt{1 + 4\ell(\ell + 1)}}{2} = \frac{-1 \mp (1 + 2\ell)}{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_1 = \ell, \quad s_2 = -(\ell + 1)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(\ell \ge 0\), \(s_2 = -(\ell + 1)\) leads to divergence at the origin \(\rho \to 0\). Retaining only the physically acceptable solution \(s = \ell\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) \sim \rho^\ell \quad \text{as } \rho \to 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Transformation \& Differential Equation for \(v(\rho)\).} Combining both asymptotic behaviors, we represent the full radial solution as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) = \rho^\ell e^{-\rho/2} v(\rho)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Writing out derivatives of \(R(\rho)\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R' = \left( \ell \rho^{\ell-1} - \frac{1}{2} \rho^\ell \right) e^{-\rho/2} v + \rho^\ell e^{-\rho/2} v'\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After expanding \(\frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{d}{d\rho} \left( \rho^2 R' \right) + R \left[ - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{\rho^2} - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{\rho_0}{\rho} \right] = 0\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}= e^{-\rho/2} \Big\{ \rho^\ell v'' + v' \left[ 2\ell \rho^{\ell-1} - \frac{1}{2} \rho^\ell + 2 \rho^{\ell-1} \right] + v \left[ \rho^\ell \ell(\ell+1) - \rho^{\ell+1} \left( \ell + 1 \right) + \frac{1}{4} \rho^{\ell+2} - \ell(\ell+1) \rho^{\ell} - \frac{1}{4} \rho^{\ell+2} + \rho_0 \rho^{\ell+1} \right] \Big\} = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dividing out non\sphinxhyphen{}zero factor \(\rho^{\ell-1} e^{-\rho/2}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho v''(\rho) + [2(\ell + 1) - \rho] v'(\rho) + (\rho_0 - \ell - 1) v(\rho) = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Polynomial expansion, energy quantization \protect\(\ E_n \ \protect\) and radial distribution \protect\(\ R_n(\rho)\protect\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Starting from the transformed radial equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho v''(\rho) + [2(\ell + 1) - \rho] v'(\rho) + (\rho_0 - \ell - 1) v(\rho) = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Looking for a power series solution:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
    v(\rho) & = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c_k \rho^k  \\
   v'(\rho) & = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k c_k \rho^{k-1} \\
  v''(\rho) & = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k(k-1) c_k \rho^{k-2} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Substituting into the differential equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k(k-1) c_k \rho^{k-1} + \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2(\ell + 1) k c_k \rho^{k-1} - \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k c_k \rho^k + (\rho_0 - \ell - 1) \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c_k \rho^k = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Shift indices to group terms by power \(\rho^k\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \Big\{ (k+1)(k) c_{k+1} + 2(\ell + 1)(k+1) c_{k+1} - k c_k + (\rho_0 - \ell - 1) c_k \Big\} \rho^k = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Recurrence Relation.} Equating coefficients to zero yields the recurrence relation for \(c_k\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_{k+1} = c_k \frac{k + \ell + 1 - \rho_0}{(k + 1)(k + 2\ell + 2)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Asymptotic Behavior \& Series Termination.} If the power series does not terminate, as \(k \to +\infty\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{c_{k+1}}{c_k} \longrightarrow \frac{1}{k}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This asymptotic behavior matches that of the exponential expansion \(e^\rho \sim \sum \frac{\rho^k}{k!}\) and thus \(\frac{c_{k+1}}{c_k} = \frac{1}{k+1} \sim \frac{1}{k}\).
Thus, an infinite series \(v(\rho) \sim e^\rho\), would lead to \(R(\rho) \sim e^{-\rho/2} e^\rho = e^{\rho/2}\), which diverges as \(\rho \to +\infty\).
Thus, in order to maintain physical normalizability, the series must terminate at a maximum power \(k_{\max} = N\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_{N+1} = 0 \implies N + \ell + 1 - \rho_0 = 0 \implies \rho_0 = N + \ell + 1 \equiv n\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N \ge 0\) is the radial quantum number.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n = N + \ell + 1\) is the \sphinxstylestrong{Principal Quantum Number} (\(n \ge 1\)).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\forall n\), the orbital angular momentum quantum number satisfies \(0 \le \ell \le n - 1\).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Energy Quantization.} Recalling the definition of \(\rho_0\), \(n = \rho_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2m}{-E}} \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 \hbar}\), and solving for the bound state energies \(E_n\) (\(E < 0\)), the relation between the energy \(E_n\) of the \(n^{th}\) energy level and the principal quantum number \(n\) follows
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:eq:atom:schrodinger:energy:details}
\begin{split}E_n = - \frac{m q^4}{32 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0^2 \hbar^2} \frac{1}{n^2} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} The value of energy \(E_n\) of Schrodinger model coincides with the value \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/bohr:eq:atom:bohr:energy} of the energy produced by {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/bohr:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-bohr}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Bohr model}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Radial solution.} Putting everything together, the radial part of the solution reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) = e^{-\rho/2} \rho^{\ell} L^{2 \ell+1}_{n-\ell-1}(\rho) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(L_{p}^{k}(x)\) the solution of the associated Laguerre differential equation \(x y'' + ( k + 1 - x ) y' + p y = 0\).
\subsubsection*{Azimuthal and polar equations}
\subsubsection*{Further separation of variables, \protect\(\ Y_{\ell m}(\theta, \varphi) = \Theta(\theta) \Phi(\varphi) \ \protect\) }

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \(Y(\theta, \varphi) = \Theta(\theta) \Psi(\varphi)\), the equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\frac{1}{Y_{lm}} \left\{ \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \partial_\theta (\sin\theta \partial_\theta Y_{lm}) + \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta} \partial_{\varphi\varphi} Y_{lm} \right\} = - \ell ( \ell + 1 ) \ . 
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
becomes \sphinxhyphen{} after multipyling by \(\sin^2 \theta\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underbrace{\frac{\sin \theta}{\Theta} \left( \sin \theta \, \Theta' \right)' + \ell ( \ell + 1 ) \, \sin^2 \theta}_{F(\theta)} = -\underbrace{\frac{\Phi''}{\Phi}}_{G(\varphi)} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F(\theta) = - G(\varphi) = m_\ell^2 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with a non\sphinxhyphen{}negative constant \(m_{\ell}^2\) in order to match periodic conditions for \(\Phi(\varphi = 0) = \Phi(\varphi = 2 \pi)\).
\subsubsection*{Azimuthal equation}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Phi'' + m_\ell^2 \Phi = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose solution is \(\Phi(\varphi) \propto \exp \left( \mp i m_{\ell} \varphi \right)\). In order to satisfy periodic conditoins, \(m_{\ell} \in \mathbb{Z}\). This parameter will be furthered constrained later, in the solution of the polar equation, to be \(m_{\ell} \in \{ - \ell, -\ell+1, \dots, \ell \}\), with \(\ell \in \mathbb{N}\). Thus, selecting only the independent solutions, the azimuthal distribution of the eigenfunctions of the Hamiltonian is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Phi(\varphi) \propto \exp\left( i m_{\ell} \varphi \right) \ , \quad m_{\ell} \in \{ - \ell, -\ell+1, \dots \ell \} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Polar equation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiplying the equation \(F(\theta) = m_{ell}^2\) by \(\Theta\), the polar equation becomes,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \sin \theta \left( \sin \theta \, \Theta' \right)' + \left[ \ell ( \ell + 1 ) \, \sin^2 \theta - m_{\ell}^2 \right] \Theta = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Polar equation as an associated Legendre equation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dividing by \(\sin^2 \theta= 1 - \cos^2 \theta\), the second term can be immediately recast as the second term in the associated Legendre equation, if \(x = \cos \theta\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(\frac{d x}{d \theta} = - \sin \theta\), then \(\frac{d}{d\theta} = \frac{d x}{d \theta} \frac{d}{d x} = - \sin \theta \frac{d}{d x}\), the first term \sphinxhyphen{} divided by \(\sin^2 \theta\) \sphinxhyphen{} becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-\frac{1}{\sin^2 \theta} \sin^2 \theta \dfrac{d}{dx} \left( - \sin^2 \theta \dfrac{d}{dx} \Theta \right) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[ ( 1 - x^2) \dfrac{d}{dx} \Theta \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the polar equation can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \frac{d}{dx} \left[ ( 1 - x^2 ) \dfrac{d \Theta}{dx} \right] + \left[ \ell(\ell+1) - \frac{m_\ell^2}{1 - x^2} \right] \Theta  \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. as the associated Legendre equation whose solution (see below) is \(\Theta(x) = P_\ell^{m_{\ell}}(x)\), for \(m_{\ell} \in \{ - \ell, \dots, \ell\}\), \(\ell \in \mathbb{N}\).
\subsubsection*{Legendre differential equation and associated Legendre equation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Legendre differential equations} read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = (1- x^2) P_n''(x) - 2 x P_n'(x) + n(n+1) P_n(x) =  \quad , \qquad x \in [-1, 1] \\
  & = \dfrac{d}{dx} \left[ ( 1-x^2 ) P_n'(x) \right] + n(n+1) P_n(x) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the solution \(P_n(x)\) be the Legendre polynomial. The \sphinxstylestrong{associated Legendre differential equations} are defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = \dfrac{d}{dx} \left[ ( 1-x^2 ) P_n'(x) \right] + \left[ n(n+1) - \frac{m^2}{1-x^2} \right] P_n(x) \quad , \qquad x \in [-1, 1] \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the solution reads \(P_{n}^{m}(x) = (-1)^{m} \left( 1 - x^2 \right)^{\frac{m}{2}} \dfrac{d^m}{dx^m} P_{n}(x)\), for \(m \ge 0\).
The soutions for \(m < 0\) are defined via symmetry conditions, or Rodrigues’ formula, as \(P_{\ell}^{-m} = (-1)^{m} \frac{(\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!} P_{\ell}^{m}(x)\), see \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated\_Legendre\_polynomials}{Wikipedia: associated Lagendre polynomials}.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Schrodinger model \sphinxhyphen{} Gallery}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:schrodinger-model-gallery}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-gallery}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery::doc}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Auxiliary Results on Operators for the Schrödinger Model of the Hydrogen Atom}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:auxiliary-results-on-operators-for-the-schrodinger-model-of-the-hydrogen-atom}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes::doc}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
All components of \(\hat{\mathbf{L}}\) commute with the kinetic term \(\frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m}\) and with \(\hat{L}^2\), {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes-commutation-l-p2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{proof}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[\hat{p}^2, \hat{L}_b] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
All components of \(\hat{\mathbf{L}}\) commute with the potential \(\hat{V}_{\text{Coulomb}}\), {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes-commutation-l-v}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{proof}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[\hat{V}_{\text{Coulomb}}, \hat{L}_b] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Therefore, all components of \(\hat{\mathbf{L}}\) commute with the \(\text{H}\) atom Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}} = \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m} + \hat{V}_{\text{Coulomb}}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}}, \hat{L}_b] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Simultaneous Commutative Set:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\boxed{[\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}}, \hat{L}^2] = 0, \quad [\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}}, \hat{L}_a] = 0, \quad [\hat{L}^2, \hat{L}_a] = 0}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}}\), total angular momentum squared \(\hat{L}^2\), and any component \(\hat{L}_a\) all mutually commute, and thus share a set of common eigenvectors. For the commutation relation \([\hat{L}^2, \hat{L}_a] = 0\), see the section about {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spatial:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum-spatial}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{spatial angular momentum}}}}.

\end{enumerate}


\subsubsection{Hamiltonian \& Basic Definitions}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:hamiltonian-basic-definitions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hamiltonian of the electron in the Hydrogen atom with Coulomb potential is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m} + \hat{V}_{Coulomb} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
that in space basis becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{H} = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \nabla^2 \langle \mathbf{r} | - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon |\mathbf{r}|} \langle \mathbf{r} | \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Space Basis Representations}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi \rangle = \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \mathbf{r} \langle \mathbf{r} | \quad \implies \quad \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{r}} | \Psi \rangle = \mathbf{r} \, \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} = -i\hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \langle \mathbf{r} | \quad \implies \quad \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi \rangle = -i\hbar \nabla \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Angular Momentum Operator}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{L}} = \hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \hat{\mathbf{p}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In Levi\sphinxhyphen{}Civita component notation, using Cartesian coordinates
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{L}} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \hat{L}_a =  \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \varepsilon_{abc} \, \hat{r}_b \hat{p}_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the space (position) basis (Cartesian coordinates):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{L}} | \Psi \rangle 
  & = \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \hat{L}_a | \Psi \rangle = \\
  & = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \varepsilon_{abc} \, r_b (-i\hbar \partial_c \langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi \rangle) = \\
  & =-i\hbar \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \varepsilon_{abc} \, r_b \, \partial_c \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) = \\
  & = - i \hbar \mathbf{r} \times \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{\protect\(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi \rangle\protect\)}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi \rangle = \int \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi \rangle \, d\mathbf{r}' = \int \delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}') \left(-i\hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}'} \Psi(\mathbf{r}', t)\right) d\mathbf{r}' = -i\hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{\protect\(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{p}_b \hat{r}_a | \Psi \rangle\protect\)}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{p}_b \hat{r}_a | \Psi \rangle = -i\hbar \partial_b \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{r}_a | \Psi \rangle  = -i\hbar \partial_b \left( r_a \langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi \rangle \right) = - i \hbar \partial_b \left( r_a \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \right) = -i\hbar (\delta_{ab} \Psi + r_a \partial_b \Psi)\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Canonical Commutation Relations (CCR)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:canonical-commutation-relations-ccr}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using postion basis and Cartesian coordinates, the CCR \([ \hat{\mathbf{r}}, \hat{\mathbf{P}} ] = i \hbar \mathbb{I}\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[r_a, p_b] \Psi = r_a (-i\hbar \partial_b \Psi) - (-i\hbar \partial_b (r_a \Psi)) = i\hbar \, \delta_{ab} \Psi \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[r_a, p_b] = i\hbar \, \delta_{ab}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Commutators of Angular Momentum with Position and Momentum}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutators-of-angular-momentum-with-position-and-momentum}}

\paragraph{Commutator \protect\([r_a, L_b]\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutator-r-a-l-b}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}r_a L_b \Psi = r_a (-i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d \Psi) = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_a r_c \partial_d \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}L_b r_a \Psi = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d (r_a \Psi) = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \delta_{ad} \Psi - i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c r_a \partial_d \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Subtracting the two expressions gives:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[r_a, L_b] \Psi = i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \delta_{ad} \Psi = i\hbar \varepsilon_{bca} \, r_c \Psi \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[r_a, L_b] =-  i \hbar \, (\mathbf{r} \times)_{a b} \, \Psi \quad \left(\text{in general } \neq 0\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{(Recall: \((\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})_i = \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j b_k = \{ \mathbf{a}_{\times} \}_{ik} \cdot \{ \mathbf{b} \}_k\), i.e. \(\{ \mathbf{a}_{\times} \}_{ik} = \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j\))}


\paragraph{Commutator \protect\([p_a, L_b]\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutator-p-a-l-b}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_a L_b \Psi = -i\hbar \partial_a \left(-i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d \Psi\right) = -\hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bcd} \, \partial_a (r_c \partial_d \Psi) = -\hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bad} \, \partial_d \Psi - \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_a \partial_d \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}L_b p_a \Psi = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d (-i\hbar \partial_a \Psi) = -\hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d \partial_a \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Subtracting the two expressions gives:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[p_a, L_b] \Psi = -\hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bad} \, \partial_d \Psi = \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{abd} \, \partial_d \Psi = i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} \, p_c \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Cartesian coordinates.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\([p_x, L_x] \equiv 0\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\([p_x, L_y] = \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{xyz} \, \partial_z \Psi = i\hbar p_z\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\([p_x, L_z] = \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{xzy} \, \partial_y \Psi = -\hbar^2 \partial_y \Psi = -i\hbar p_y\)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\paragraph{Commutator \protect\([\hat{p}^2, L_b]\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutator-hat-p-2-l-b}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes-commutation-l-p2}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[p^2, L_b] = \sum_a p_a p_a L_b - L_b \sum_a p_a p_a = \sum_a \Big( p_a [p_a, L_b] + [p_a, L_b] p_a \Big)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using \([p_a, L_b] = i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} p_c\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_a \left( p_a (i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} p_c) + (i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} p_c) p_a \right) = i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} (p_a p_c + p_c p_a)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(p_a p_c = p_c p_a\) (symmetric in \(a, c\)) and \(\varepsilon_{abc}\) is antisymmetric in \(a, c\), the sum vanishes identically:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[p^2, L_b] = 0 \quad \text{for all components } b\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Example.} For \(b = x\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[p^2, L_x] = -i\hbar^3 \Big[ 1 \cdot \partial_z \partial_y \Psi - 1 \cdot \partial_y \partial_z \Psi \Big] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Commutator of Coulomb Potential \protect\(\hat{V}\protect\) with Angular Momentum \protect\(\hat{L}_b\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutator-of-coulomb-potential-hat-v-with-angular-momentum-hat-l-b}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes-commutation-l-v}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In space basis, the Coulomb potential reads:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{V} | \Psi \rangle = -\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{1}{r} \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t) = -k \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s evaluate whether \(\hat{V}\) and \(\hat{L}_b\) commute:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Action of \(\hat{V} \hat{L}_b\):}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{V} \hat{L}_b | \Psi \rangle = -k \frac{1}{\sqrt{x_a x_a}} \left( -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \, \partial_d \Psi \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Action of \(\hat{L}_b \hat{V}\), with \(|\mathbf{r}| = \sqrt{ x_a x_a }\):}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{L}_b \hat{V} | \Psi \rangle = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \, \partial_d \left( -k \frac{\Psi}{\sqrt{x_a x_a}} \right) = i\hbar k \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \left[ -\frac{\partial_d |\mathbf{r}|}{|\mathbf{r}|^2} \Psi + \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \partial_d \Psi \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(\partial_d | \mathbf{r}| = \partial_d \sqrt{x_a x_a} = \frac{x_d}{|\mathbf{r}|}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{L}_b \hat{V} | \Psi \rangle = i\hbar k \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \left[ -\frac{r_d}{|\mathbf{r}|^3} \Psi + \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \partial_d \Psi \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Commutator \([\hat{V}, \hat{L}_b]\):}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | [\hat{V}, \hat{L}_b] | \Psi \rangle = -i\hbar k \, \frac{\varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c r_d}{|\mathbf{r}|^3} \Psi = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Why?} The product \(r_c r_d\) is \sphinxstylestrong{symmetric} under swapping \(c \leftrightarrow d\), while \(\varepsilon_{bcd}\) is \sphinxstylestrong{antisymmetric} under swapping \(c \leftrightarrow d\). Summing over \(c, d\) gives zero!

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Example for \(b = x\).} \(\varepsilon_{xcd} r_c r_d = \varepsilon_{xyz} y z + \varepsilon_{xzy} z y = yz - zy = 0\).

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxstepscope

\section{Introduction to the QM of Solids}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:introduction-to-the-qm-of-solids}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:semiconductors-solids-qm}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm::doc}}

\subsection{Energy bands}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:energy-bands}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:semiconductors-solids-qm-energy-bands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
First, the energy level splitting is discussed. Then, two models (Kronig\sphinxhyphen{}Penny, and nearly free electron models) are introduced to describe the concept of allowed and forbidden energy bands, starting from Schrodinger equation.


\subsubsection{Energy level splitting}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:energy-level-splitting}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section deal with energy level splitting in a two\sphinxhyphen{}element system.
\subsubsection*{Non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting systems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(| L \rangle\), and \(| R \rangle\) two localized eigen\sphinxhyphen{}states of non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting identical subsystems, with the same energy \(E_0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{H}_0 | L \rangle & = E_0 | L \rangle  \\
  \hat{H}_0 | R \rangle & = E_0 | R \rangle  \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As these states are localized in space, they’re (approximately?) orthogonal, \(\langle L | R \rangle = 0\).
\subsubsection*{Interacting subsystems \sphinxhyphen{} Perturbation potential}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the two systems are brought close together, they start interacting weakly, so that the Hamiltonian becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \hat{V} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The matrix elements of the Hamiltonian in the base \(\left\{ | L \rangle, | R \rangle \right\}\) (where are all the other eigen\sphinxhyphen{}functions? We’re not interested in them, right now, but only on the pair of eigenfunctions with the same energy when the syb\sphinxhyphen{}systems are not interacting) read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle L | \hat{H} | L \rangle & =: E_0' \\
  \langle R | \hat{H} | R \rangle & =: E_0' \\
  \langle L | \hat{H} | R \rangle & = \langle R | \hat{H} | L \rangle^* =: -t \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Energy levels \sphinxhyphen{} Eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian operator }

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the new eigen\sphinxhyphen{}functions of the interacting system can be written as a linear combination of the non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting functions, \(| \Psi_{1,2} \rangle= \ell_{1,2} | L \rangle + r_{1,2} | R \rangle\), the eigen\sphinxhyphen{}problem becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} | \Psi_{1,2} \rangle = E_{1,2} | \Psi_{1,2} \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Projecting onto \(\langle L |\), and \(\langle R |\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{cases}
     \ell E_0' - r t    = E \ell \\
   - \ell t    + r E_0' = E r    \\
\end{cases}
\quad \rightarrow \quad
\begin{cases}
     \ell (E_0'-E) - r t    = 0 \\
   - \ell t    + r (E_0'-E) = 0 \\
\end{cases}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This system has non trivial solutions, if the determinant of the linear system is zero,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \left| \begin{matrix} E_0' - E & -t \\ -t & E_0' - E \end{matrix}\right| = ( E_0' - E ) - t^2 \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy levels of the interacting states are slightly shifted w.r.t. the non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting level,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = E_0' \mp t \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Eigen\sphinxhyphen{}states}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The eigen\sphinxhyphen{}states are
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{bonding state}, for \(E = E_0' - t\), \(\ell = -r\), and with normalization
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle_{-} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( | L \rangle + | R \rangle \right) \ \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{anti\sphinxhyphen{}bonding state}, for \(E = E_0' + t\), \(\ell = r\), and with normalization
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle_{+} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( | L \rangle - | R \rangle \right) \ \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Kronig\sphinxhyphen{}Penny model}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:kronig-penny-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:semiconductors-solids-qm-energy-bands-kronig-penny}}\subsubsection*{Kronig\sphinxhyphen{}Penny potential}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Kronig\sphinxhyphen{}Penny model is a 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional model with periodic square wave potential,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V(x) = \left\{\begin{aligned}
  V_0  \quad & , \quad x \in \text{regions II} = [ n a + (n-1) b, n ( a + b )]  \\
    0  \quad & , \quad x \in \text{regions I } = [ (n-1) (a+b), n a + (n-1) b] \\
\end{aligned}\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{General expression of Bloch states}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/solid-state/notes-solid-state:solid-state-crystals-bloch-thm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Bloch’s theorem}}}}, the eigen\sphinxhyphen{}states of an electron (in position base) in a infinite periodic lattice can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Psi(\mathbf{r}) = u(\mathbf{r}) e^{i \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(u(\mathbf{r}) = u \left(\mathbf{r} + \sum_j n_j \mathbf{a}_i \right)\) with the same periodicity as the lattice, \(n_j \in \mathbb{Z}\), or in 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Psi(x) = u(x) e^{i k x} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Eigenvalue problem for the Hamiltonian operator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The eigenvalue problem for the Hamiltonian operator reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E \Psi = \hat{H}  \Psi = \left[ \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m} + V(x) \right] \Psi \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\hat{p}\) the momentum operator, whose expression in position base is given by \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:eq:qm:momentum-operator}, and in 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems \(\hat{p} \Psi = - i \hbar \partial_x \Psi\). The operator acting twice gives \(\hat{p}^2 \Psi = - \hbar^2 \partial_{xx} \Psi\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Introducing the expression of the eigenfunctions from Bloch’s theorem%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
The derivatives read \(\Psi' = \left( u' + i k u \right) e^{i k x}\), and \(\Psi'' = \left( u'' + 2 ik u' - k^2 u \right) e^{ikx}\).
%
\end{footnote}, it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E u(x) = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \left( u''(x) + 2 ik u'(x) - k^2 u(x)  \right) + V(x) u(x) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 & = u'' + 2 i k u'(x) - \left( k^2 - \frac{2m E}{\hbar^2} \right) u(x) && \text{regions I} \\
  0 & = u'' + 2 i k u'(x) - \left( k^2 - \frac{2m ( E - V_0 )}{\hbar^2} \right) u(x) && \text{regions II} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Solution of the ODEs.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Continuity of \(\Psi(x)\), and \(\partial_x \Psi(x)\).} for matching solutions.**

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Energy levels.}

\subsection{Structure of a semi\sphinxhyphen{}semiconductor}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:structure-of-a-semi-semiconductor}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, \(N_A\), \(N_D\), \(N_A^-\), \(N_D^+\) only depends on the space coordinate, as a consequencen of doping. The concentration of free electrons and holes may be time dependent instead (…).


\subsubsection{Intrinsic semiconductor}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:intrinsic-semiconductor}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-intrinsic}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Lattice of \(\text{Si}\) atoms. Some free electrons have left the valence bands of the atoms and entered the conduction band. For a new free electron, a new hole is left behind in the lattice. If the medium is \sphinxstylestrong{electrically neutral} the numbers of free electrons and holes are locally equal, and thus their concentrations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n_i(\mathbf{r}) = p_i(\mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Doped semiconductors}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:doped-semiconductors}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped}}

\paragraph{\protect\(p\protect\)\sphinxhyphen{}type}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:p-type}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-p-type}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The semiconductor is doped with atoms of class \(\text{III}\), replacing some of the \(\text{Si}\) atoms in the lattice. These atoms introduce a hole in the lattice and are prone to collect \(e^-\) from neighboring \(\text{Si}\) atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-full-ionization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{full\sphinxhyphen{}ionization condition}}}}, all the doping atoms are ionized, and thus \(N_A^- = N_A\). In a \sphinxstylestrong{electrically netural} region with no donor atoms, the concentration of the holes is equal to the sum of the concentration of the ionized acceptor atoms and the free electrons,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p = n + N_A^- \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In a standard \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}type semiconductor, \(N_A >> n_i\), and thus \(p \sim N_A^-\).


\paragraph{\protect\(n\protect\)\sphinxhyphen{}type}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:n-type}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-n-type}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The semiconductor is doped with atoms of class \(\text{V}\), replacing some of the \(\text{Si}\) atoms in the lattice. These atoms introduce a “extra” loosely bound electron in the lattice and are prone to release it in the conduction band of the semiconductor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-full-ionization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{full\sphinxhyphen{}ionization condition}}}}, all the doping atoms are ionized, and thus \(N_D^+ = N_D\). In a \sphinxstylestrong{electrically netural} region with no acceptor atoms, the concentration of the free electrons is equal to the sum of the concentration of the ionized donor atoms and holes,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n = p + N_D^+ \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In a standard \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}type semiconductor, \(N_D >> p_i\), and thus \(n \sim N_D^+\).


\paragraph{Full ionization}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:full-ionization}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-full-ionization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo}


\subsection{Electric charge density}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:electric-charge-density}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-charge-density}}\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:eq:semi:charge-density}
\begin{split}\rho(\mathbf{r},t) = -q n(\mathbf{r},t) + q p(\mathbf{r},t) + q N_D^+(\mathbf{r},t) - q N_A^-(\mathbf{r},t) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(q\) the elementary charge, the charge of the electron (here the opposite to get a positive numerical value of \(q\) in Coulomb)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n(\mathbf{r},t)\) the number volume density of the mobile electrons

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(p(\mathbf{r},t)\) the number volume density of the holes in the valence bands of the lattice

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N_D^+(\mathbf{r},t)\) the number volume density of the positive donor ions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N_A^-(\mathbf{r},t)\) the number volume density of the negative acceptor ions

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, \(N_D^+(\mathbf{r})\), \(N_A^-(\mathbf{r})\), corresponding to the density of the donor and acceptor atoms in the lattice, that have fixed positions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} \sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Discuss the values of \(N_D^+\) and \(N_D\) in terms of energy levels at different temperatures.} Add this discussion to {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-full-ionization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{full\sphinxhyphen{}ionization section}}}} or in another section and then point to it?

\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:carrier-transport-phenomena}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:semiconductors-transport-phenomena}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In this section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Currents in semiconductors}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:currents-in-semiconductors}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:semiconductors-transport-phenomena-currents}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Two main processes:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{diffusion} due to non\sphinxhyphen{}uniform density

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{drift} due to an electric field \(\mathbf{e}(\mathbf{r})\)

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The overall current has the contribution of the motion of both electrons (\(n\), for negative charges) and holes (\(p\), for positive “charges”),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{j}(\mathbf{r},t) = \mathbf{j}_n(\mathbf{r},t) + \mathbf{j}_p(\mathbf{r},t) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and both these contributions have their diffusion and drift part,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{j}_n & = \mathbf{j}_{n,diff} + \mathbf{j}_{n,drift} \\
  \mathbf{j}_p & = \mathbf{j}_{p,diff} + \mathbf{j}_{p,drift} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the contribution of the electrons, the diffusion current follows a Fick’s law for the number density \(n\) (multiplied by the constant charge \(-q\) of the elementary charge), while the drift coefficient is written as the product of the negative charge density and their drift velocity,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-n}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{j}_n 
  & = \mathbf{j}_{n,diff} + \mathbf{j}_{n,drift} = \\
  & = - D_n (-q) \nabla n + \underbrace{(-q) n}_{\rho_n} \mathbf{v}_n = \\
  & = D_n q \nabla n + q \mu_n n \mathbf{e} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being the average drift velocity, \(\mathbf{v}_n = - \mu_n \mathbf{e}\), a function on the local electric field through the electron mobility \(\mu_n\). Here the minus sign follows the definition of the electron mobility with positive value, and from the opposite direction of the local electric field \(\mathbf{e}\) and the drift velocity of negative charges.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the contribution of the holes,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-p}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{j}_p 
  & = - D_p q \nabla p + q \mu_p p \mathbf{e} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}

\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{|T|T|T|}
\hline

\sphinxAtStartPar

&\sphinxstyletheadfamily 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\\

\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} While charges in free\sphinxhyphen{}space have acceleration proportional to the electric field, in solids they have drift velocity proportional to the electric field, due to collisions with the lattice. This mechanism can be described in terms of conductivity \(\sigma\) (or its inverse, resistivity \(\rho_R\)) of the medium, similarly to Ohm’s law
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{j} = \sigma \mathbf{e} \quad , \quad \mathbf{e} = \rho_R \mathbf{j} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the expression of the drift current, as the sum of the \(n\) and \(p\) contributions in \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-n} and \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-p} respectively,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{j}_{drift} = q ( \mu_n n + \mu_p p ) \mathbf{e} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it immediatley follows the formula for the resistivity (and the conductivity)
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:resistivity}
\begin{split}\rho_R = \frac{1}{\sigma} = \frac{1}{q (\mu_n n + \mu_p p)} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{See discussion about this relation in 5.1.4. Velocity Saturation}


\subsection{Einstein relation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:einstein-relation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:semiconductors-transport-phenomena-einstein-relation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
…
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:einstein-relation}
\begin{split}\frac{D_n}{\mu_n} = \frac{D_p}{\mu_p} = \frac{k T}{q} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}

\subsection{Balance equations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:balance-equations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:semiconductors-transport-phenomena-equations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The density of free electrons and holes are governed by the following PDEs
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:num-balance}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t n - \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\mathbf{j}_n}{q} \right) = ( G_n - R_n ) \\
  & \partial_t p + \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\mathbf{j}_p}{q} \right) = ( G_p - R_p ) \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the expression of current densities \(\mathbf{j}_n\), \(\mathbf{j}_p\) are given in \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-n}, \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-p} respectively, and the terms \(G_{n,p}\), \(R_{n,p}\) represent source and sink terms representing \sphinxstylestrong{generation} or \sphinxstylestrong{recombination} of free charges and holes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As for a new free electron there’s a new hole, then \(G_n = G_p\). As recombination occurs between the same number of free electrons and holes, \(R_n = R_g\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiplying the first and the second equation in \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:num-balance} by \(-q\) and \(q\) respectively, the balance equation for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{free} charge density \(\rho_f = - q n + q p\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_t \rho_f + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j} = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope

\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-non-equilibrium:non-equilibrium-excess-carriers-in-semiconductors}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-non-equilibrium:semiconductors-non-equilibrium}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-non-equilibrium::doc}}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{\protect\(p\protect\)\sphinxhyphen{}\protect\(n\protect\) Junctions}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:p-n-junctions}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:semiconductors-pn-junctions}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions::doc}}



\subsection{Introduction to the pn Junction and its Operational Regimes}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:introduction-to-the-pn-junction-and-its-operational-regimes}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:semiconductors-pn-junctions-regimes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When a \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}type and an \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}type semiconductor are brought into intimate contact, the immense carrier concentration gradients at the interface drive a transient diffusion process. Mobile electrons and holes annihilate each other at the metallurgical interface, leaving behind uncompensated, fixed dopant ions. This region, stripped of mobile carriers, is known as the \sphinxstylestrong{depletion region}. The fixed charges generate an internal electric field that opposes further diffusion, establishing a balance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on the external voltage \(V_a\) applied across the device, the junction operates in one of three primary regimes:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Zero Bias (Thermal Equilibrium, \(V_a = 0\)):} No external voltage is applied. The internal electric field perfectly balances the carrier diffusion gradients. The net current density for both electrons and holes is identically zero (\(J_n = 0, J_p = 0\)).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Forward Bias (\(V_a > 0\)):} A positive potential is applied to the \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}side relative to the \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}side. This external potential opposes the built\sphinxhyphen{}in field, lowering the electrostatic barrier and narrowing the depletion width. Diffusion forces win over drift, resulting in an exponential injection of minority carriers across the junction.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reverse Bias (\(V_a < 0\)):} A negative potential is applied to the \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}side relative to the \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}side. The external voltage reinforces the built\sphinxhyphen{}in field, widening the depletion region and increasing the potential barrier. Diffusion drops to zero, and the current is limited to a minute reverse saturation current driven by thermal generation.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{The Depletion Approximation and Shockley Transport}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:the-depletion-approximation-and-shockley-transport}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:semiconductors-pn-junctions-depletion-approximation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To derive closed\sphinxhyphen{}form analytical expressions for the electrostatics and current\sphinxhyphen{}voltage relations, we employ the \sphinxstylestrong{Depletion Approximation} (also called the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Abrupt Junction Approximation}). This framework assumes that the transition between doping zones is perfectly sharp and that the depletion region is completely devoid of mobile carriers (\(\rho = \text{constant}\) inside the zone, \(\rho = 0\) outside).

\subsubsection{Zero Bias (Thermal Equilibrium)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:zero-bias-thermal-equilibrium}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:semiconductors-pn-junctions-depletion-approximation-zero-bias}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By applying the depletion approximation, the net space\sphinxhyphen{}charge density \(\rho(x)\) is treated as piecewise constant:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho(x) = \begin{cases} 
  0 & x \lt x_p \\
 -q N_A & x_p \le x < 0 \\
  q N_D & 0 \le x \le x_n \\
  0 & x \gt x_n \ .
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integrating Gauss’ law, \(\partial_x e(x) = \frac{\rho(x)}{\varepsilon}\), with the assumption of electrical neutrality, \(0 = q (N_A x_p + N_D x_n)\), and zero field outside the interface,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}e(x) = \begin{cases}
  0 & x \lt x_p \\
  -\frac{q N_A}{\varepsilon} \left( x - x_p \right) & x_p \le x < 0 \\
   \frac{q N_D}{\varepsilon} \left( x - x_n \right) & 0 \le x \le x_n \\
  0 & x \gt x_n \ .
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integrating the relation between the electric field and the electric potential, \(e(x) = - \partial_x \phi(x)\), with the reference \(\phi(x) = 0\) in the \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk, \(x < x_p\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\phi(x) = \begin{cases}
  0 & x \lt x_p \\
  \frac{q N_A}{2 \varepsilon} \left( x - x_p \right)^2 & x_p \le x < 0 \\
  \frac{q N_D}{2 \varepsilon} \left( x - x_n  \right)^2 + \frac{q N_A}{2 \varepsilon} x_p^2 - \frac{q N_D}{2 \varepsilon} x_n^2 & 0 \le x \le x_n \\
  \frac{q}{2 \varepsilon} \left( N_A x_p^2 - N_D x_n^2 \right) =: V_{bi} & x \gt x_n \ .
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Global charge neutrality requires \(-N_A x_p = N_D x_n\), yielding the equilibrium depletion width \(W_0\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}W_0 = x_p + x_n = \sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon_s V_{bi}}{q} \left( \frac{1}{N_A} + \frac{1}{N_D} \right)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the continuity of the potential, for \(0 \le x \le x_n\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \phi(x) 
  & = - \frac{q N_D}{\varepsilon} \left[ \frac{x^2}{2} - x_n x \right] + \phi(0) = \\
  & = - \frac{q N_D}{\varepsilon} \left[ \frac{x^2}{2} - x_n x \right] + \frac{q N_A}{2 \varepsilon} x_p^2 = \\
  & = - \frac{q N_D}{2 \varepsilon} \left( x - x_n  \right)^2 + \frac{q N_A}{2 \varepsilon} x_p^2 + \frac{q N_D}{2 \varepsilon} x_n^2
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the potential difference across the depletion region \(V_{bi}\) reads,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \phi(x_n) = \frac{q}{2 \varepsilon} \left( N_A x_p^2 + N_D x_n^2 \right) =: V_{bi} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The width of the depletion region be \(w\) can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  w 
  & = x_n - x_p = \\ 
  & = x_n \left( 1 + \frac{N_D}{N_A} \right)
    = x_n N_D \left( \frac{1}{N_D} + \frac{1}{N_A} \right) = \\
  & = - x_p \left( \frac{N_A}{N_D} + 1 \right) 
    = - x_p N_A \left( \frac{1}{N_D} + \frac{1}{N_A} \right) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
then the potential can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  V_{bi}
  & = \frac{q}{2 \varepsilon} \left( \frac{N_A^2 x_p^2}{N_A} + \frac{N_D^2 x_n^2}{N_D} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{q}{2 \varepsilon} N_A^2 x_p^2 \left( \frac{1}{N_A} + \frac{1}{N_D} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{q}{2 \varepsilon} w^2 \left( \frac{1}{N_A} + \frac{1}{N_D} \right)^{-1} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the width of the depletion region can be written as a function of the built\sphinxhyphen{}in potential as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}w = \sqrt{\frac{2 \varepsilon V_{bi}}{q} \left( \frac{1}{N_A} + \frac{1}{N_D} \right)} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Deal with some statistical mechanics to show this}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The total voltage drop across the region is the \sphinxstylestrong{built\sphinxhyphen{}in potential} \(V_{bi}\), determined by the bulk doping concentrations and the Law of Mass Action (\(n_0 p_0 = n_i^2\)):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V_{bi} = V_t \ln\left(\frac{N_A N_D}{n_i^2}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(V_t = \frac{k_B T}{q}\) is the thermal voltage.


\subsubsection{Forward Bias Under Shockley Assumptions}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:forward-bias-under-shockley-assumptions}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:semiconductors-pn-junctions-depletion-approximation-fwd-bias}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To find the explicit \(I\text{-}V\) relationship, we introduce the \sphinxstylestrong{Shockley Ideal Conditions}:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Low\sphinxhyphen{}level injection (\(n \ll N_A\) in the \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk; \(p \ll N_D\) in the \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
No recombination or generation occurs inside the depletion region.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The electric field in the neutral bulk regions is negligible; transport there is purely diffusion\sphinxhyphen{}driven.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Width of the depletion region.}
The applied forward voltage \(V_a\) lowers the barrier, modifying the depletion width to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}W(V_a) = \sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon_s (V_{bi} - V_a)}{q} \left( \frac{1}{N_A} + \frac{1}{N_D} \right)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Minority charge injection.} Lowering the barrier causes minority charge injection at the boundaries of the depletion region. Compared to the equilibrium condition with no external voltage,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \Delta n(x_p) & = n_{p0} \left[ \exp\left( \frac{V_a}{V_t} \right) - 1 \right] \\
  \Delta p(x_n) & = p_{n0} \left[ \exp\left( \frac{V_a}{V_t} \right) - 1 \right] \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Charge transport dynamics.} If Shockley conditions hold, no recombination in the depletion region occurs; recombination occurs in the bulk of \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{} and \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{} sections: in bulk regions, the electric field \(\vec{e}\) is negligible, and thus the current is driven by diffusion only.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Governing equation of the holes in the \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk immediately follows from equation \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:num-balance}, with the assumption of no drift current in \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-p},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \partial_t \Delta p_n  
  & = - \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{j_{p,diff}}{q} \right) + \Delta ( G - R ) = \\
  & = - \nabla \cdot \left( - D \Delta p_n \nabla n \right) + \Delta ( G - R ) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or in 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems with constant coefficients
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_t \Delta p_n = D \partial_{xx} \Delta p_n + \Delta ( G - R )\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming \sphinxstyleemphasis{steady\sphinxhyphen{}state diffusion equation} (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{justify this limit}) governs the diffusion of the minority charge carriers in the bulk, and using \sphinxstylestrong{the law of mass action} to write the source term (see box below), the governing equation becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D_p \Delta p_n'' = \frac{1}{\tau_p} \Delta p_n \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\tau_p = \frac{1}{k_r n_{n0}}\).
\subsubsection*{Law of mass action for \protect\(\ G - R\protect\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk region,
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n_{n0} \gg p_{n0}\),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\Delta n = \Delta p\) if the electrical charge remains zero

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\Delta p_n \gg p_{n0}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\Delta n_n \ll n_{n0}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the source term becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
R - G 
& = k_r p n - k_r p_0 n_0 = \\
& = k_r ( p_{n0} + \Delta p_n ) ( n_{n0} + \Delta n_n ) - k_r p_{n0} n_{n0} = \\
& = k_r ( p_{n0} \Delta n_n + n_{n0} \Delta p_n + \Delta n_n \Delta p_n ) = \\
& \simeq k_r n_{n0} \Delta p_n
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
as:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(G \sim G_0 = R_0\) at equilibrium. \sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Find some time/space to justify all these sentences about equilibrium}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the conditions at the beginning of the box give:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n_{n0} \Delta p_n \gg p_{n0} \Delta n_n\) (because the deltas are equal, and \(n_{n0} \gg p_{n0}\))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n_{n0} \Delta p_n \gg \Delta p_n \Delta n_n\) (because the deltas are equal, and \(n_{n0} \gg \Delta n_{n}\)

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The differential porblem supplied with proper boundary conditions becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \frac{\Delta p_n(x)}{\tau_p} = D_p \Delta p''_n(x) \\
  & p(x_n) = p_{n0} \left[  \exp\left( \frac{V_a}{V_t} \right) - 1 \right] \\
  & p(x \rightarrow +\infty) = 0 \\
\end{aligned} \right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and its solution reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta p_n(x) = p_{n0} \left[ \exp \left( \frac{V_a}{V_t} \right) - 1 \right] \exp\left( - \frac{x - x_n}{L_p} \right) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(L_p = \sqrt{ \tau_p D_p }\) for the holes in the \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk, \(x > x_n\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta n_p(x) = n_{p0} \left[ \exp \left( \frac{V_a}{V_t} \right) - 1 \right] \exp\left( \frac{x - x_p}{L_n} \right) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(L_n = \sqrt{ \tau_n D_n }\) for the electrons in the \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk, \(x < x_p\).%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
The boundary conditions of the diffusion of \(n\) in the \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk are \(n(x \rightarrow -\infty) = 0\), \(n(x_p) = n_{p0} [ \dots ]\).
%
\end{footnote}%
\begin{footnote}[2]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
Usually \(n_0 \ll \Delta n \ll N_A\).
%
\end{footnote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Current under steady conditions.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Depletion region \(x \in [x_n, x_p]\). Under steady conditions, no charge accumulation occurs along the \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}\(n\) junction and thus the current must be constant. There’s no recombination or generation inside the depletion region \(x \in [x_p, x_n]\), thus the following conditions hold for holes and free electrons
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     \text{const} & = A J_p(x) = A J_p(x_p) = A J_p(x_n)  \quad \forall x \in [x_p, x_n] \\
     \text{const} & = A J_n(x) = A J_n(x_p) = A J_n(x_n) \ ,
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{const} = A J(x) \quad \forall x \in [x_p, x_n] \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Evaluating the current at the boundary of the depletion region (in the model, just ouside that, so that the electric field is zero and the current is driven only by diffusion)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     I = A J(x)
     & = A J_n(x) + A J_p(x) = \\
     & = A J_n(x_p) + A J_p(x_n) = \\
     & = - A (-q) D_n n_p'(x_p) - A q D_p p_n'(x_n) = \\
     & = A q D_n \frac{1}{L_n} n_{p0} \left[ \exp \left( \frac{V_a}{V_t} \right) - 1 \right] + A q D_p \frac{1}{L_p} p_{n0} \left[ \exp \left( \frac{V_a}{V_t} \right) - 1 \right] = \\
     & = q A \left( \frac{D_n n_{p0}}{L_n} + \frac{D_p p_{n0}}{L_p} \right) \left[ \exp \left( \frac{V_a}{V_t} \right) - 1 \right] \ .
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This equation readily gives the \(V(I)\) relation for an ideal \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}\(n\) junction,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-pn-junctions:eq:semiconductors:pn-junction:iv}
\begin{split} I(V) = I_0 \left[ \exp \left( \frac{V}{V_t} \right) - 1  \right] \ , \end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(I_0 = q A \left( \dots \right) = q A n_i^2 \left( \frac{D_n}{L_n N_A} + \frac{D_p}{L_p N_D} \right)\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk, \(x \in [ x_n, +\infty)\). In this region, the electric field is assumed to be negligible, and thus only diffusion drives the current of the charge carriers. For the holes,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     J_p(x) 
     & = - D_p p'_n(x) = \\
     & = \frac{D_p}{L_p} p_{n0} \exp\left( \frac{V_a}{V_t} \right) \exp \left( - \frac{x-x_n}{L_p} \right) = \\
     & = J_p(x_n) \exp \left( - \frac{x-x_n}{L_p} \right)  \ .
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus \(J_n(x) = J - J_p(x)\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}bulk, \(x \in (-\infty, x_p]\)…

\end{itemize}
